title: The Choice Is Personal. The Conversation Can Be Shared.
subtitle: An additional Daily Read: A calm conversation about posthumous organ-donation wishes can help relatives understand one another without turning anyone’s choice into a family vote.

body: A conversation, not a decision for everyone

Talking about organ donation can sound like a conversation about death, paperwork or a decision the family must make together. It can be simpler and more personal than that: each adult gets a chance to say what they want others to understand about their own wishes, what they are unsure about, or whether they would rather not discuss it. The point is not to reach agreement. It is to make room for people to be heard.

This story is about posthumous donation—donation after a person’s death—not living donation, in which someone considers donating an organ while alive. It is also not a family vote, a registration process or a way to settle an urgent hospital decision in advance. Each person’s preference belongs to that person. Relatives can listen, ask what someone means and remember what they heard without taking ownership of the choice.
What the survey says—and what it doesn’t

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ 2025 National Survey of Organ Donation Attitudes and Practices included 10,008 adults surveyed between September 2024 and February 2025. In the report, 49% said they had heard a family member’s wishes about donation. Respondents were more likely to say they would donate a family member’s organs if that person’s wishes were known than if the wishes were unknown: 85% compared with 69% [1].

Those are survey responses, not a prediction of what any particular family will do. They do, however, point to a practical reason to talk: relatives may find it easier to understand a person’s wishes when they have heard them directly. Sharing a preference does not require anyone else to share it. And uncertainty is a real answer, not a failure to finish the conversation.

Donation conversations in clinical settings are not the same as conversations at home. Research on clinical conversations can still remind us to approach this subject with care, as long as we do not mistake it for proof that a particular family exercise works. A qualitative study in eight Dutch hospitals observed 29 donation conversations and included interviews with 24 family members. The researchers described concerns involving grief, time, procedural clarity and whether other relatives were involved [2]. These circumstances are distinct from a calm family discussion, but they underscore why pressure and ambiguity can make a hard subject harder.

A separate qualitative study, conducted with participants in two hospitals in Chile, examined the emotional and relational complexity of conversations with bereaved families [3]. Its setting matters; it should not be treated as a universal guide to how families talk. Together, these studies counsel humility rather than a formula. A thoughtful conversation at home cannot remove the difficulty of a future loss, but it can give people a chance to share what they mean while they are able to do so.
Choose a moment that has room for the subject

There is no need to stage a solemn family meeting or spring the topic on someone during a health scare. Choose an ordinary, unhurried moment when people can leave or change the subject. A meal after the plates are cleared, a quiet visit or a planned call may work better than a holiday gathering with a packed agenda. If the family has experienced a recent death or donation-related distress, consider whether now is a kind time to raise it—or whether waiting would be better.

Start by asking permission: “Would you be comfortable talking about organ-donation wishes for a few minutes? It’s fine to pass.” That opening does important work. It makes the subject explicit, gives everyone a choice about taking part and signals that no one is being asked to make a decision on the spot. If someone says no, accept it without asking them to justify the answer.
Let each person speak in their own terms

If people are willing, invite each adult to speak for themselves. A useful prompt is: “What would you want your family to understand about your wishes—or what are you still unsure about?” One person might have a settled preference; another may want more information; someone else may not want to discuss the subject today. These answers can sit alongside one another without being ranked.

Listeners can reflect rather than rebut: “What I hear you saying is…” Then ask, “Did I get that right?” This helps distinguish what a person actually said from what a relative fears they meant. If a concern comes up, make room for it without treating the conversation as a debate to win. Qualitative research in different clinical and cultural settings describes families with differing views and complex communication dynamics; it does not establish one approach that will suit everyone [2][3]. Listening carefully is a reasonable starting point, not a guaranteed solution.

People may wonder what donation involves, how a preference is recorded or whether their health history affects eligibility. You do not have to answer those questions from memory, and no one should be pressed to settle them during a family discussion. Write down what someone wants to learn and, if they choose, look for current information through official organ-donation resources. Details about how preferences are recorded can depend on where a person lives, so check the relevant official information rather than assuming one process applies everywhere.

The conversation itself is not registration. If someone wants to record or change their own preference, that is a separate step for that individual to explore. A relative can offer to sit nearby or help find information only if asked. Keep the distinction clear: listening to someone’s wishes is not the same as speaking for them, and a family conversation does not authorize one person to decide for another.
A brief conversation with a clear boundary

For a first try, set aside 10–15 minutes and agree that anyone can pass or stop. Ask permission, then give each willing adult a turn to answer the same open question: “What would you want us to understand about your wishes, or what is still unclear?” Let people finish. Reflect back one point in your own words and check whether you understood. Avoid asking someone to defend a yes, a no or a not-yet.

Before you begin, say that the goal is understanding, not agreement or completing paperwork. If discussion becomes tense, pause; the subject can be revisited only if people want that. Close by asking whether anyone wants to keep a question for later. No one has to promise a follow-up, share more than they choose or make the conversation a recurring family assignment.
Leave the choice with the person

At the end, make space for different answers to remain different. One relative may have learned something important; another may still be undecided; someone else may have chosen not to take part. None of those outcomes needs a verdict. If a person wants to act on their own preference, let them name the next step and decide whether they want help finding official information. If they do not, let the conversation end there.

For a first conversation, try one question and one round of listening—not a family pledge or a registration session. Each adult can say what they want understood, or pass. The listener can reflect back what they heard and ask if it is accurate. Then stop. If a question remains, write it down only with that person’s agreement. The useful result may simply be that people know where one another stands, or that they have permission to leave the subject open.
